_comment: Company Brain realm, as configuration in the repository rather than as clicks in an
admin console. Task id M1.1.1.
WHY THIS FILE EXISTS. A Keycloak realm configured by hand is a permission-adjacent
system whose current state nobody can diff, review or restore. Every value below is a
decision, and several of them are the difference between a working sign-in and a
silent bypass, so they belong where a reviewer sees them change.
IMPORTED AND VERIFIED on 2026-09-06 against Keycloak 26.0, which is what this file
had been waiting for. The earlier note here said it had never been imported and that
M1.1.1 could not be called done until it was. It has been now, so that note is gone
and this is what happened.
The import ran on a throwaway server, as the note asked: an ephemeral container bound
to localhost with a memory limit, never registered with Coolify, removed afterwards.
Keycloak reported 'Realm brain imported' and 'Import finished successfully'.
The first attempt logged three warnings and they were real: 'Referenced client scope
openid doesn't exist. Ignoring', and the same for profile and email. brain-console
listed all three and this file defines none of them, because a full import replaces
the client scope set with the one declared here. They are removed; see the note on
defaultClientScopes. The second import was silent.
What the server actually stored was then read back rather than assumed: RS256, the
ten-hour session, refresh revocation with no reuse, brute-force protection, no
password grant and no implicit flow on any client, PKCE S256 on the public one, and
the whole group tree including the scoped subgroups under approver and
department-admin. All of it matches what is written here.
One thing is still untested: ops/keycloak/setup.sh. The import above mounted this file
and started the server with --import-realm; it did not go through kcadm. The script's
own header says it has never been run and that remains true.
Realm JSON is version-sensitive. This was verified on 26.0; expect a different major
version to reject or ignore fields.
THE SETTINGS THAT MATTER, AND WHY:
defaultSignatureAlgorithm RS256, and every client pinned to it. brain.identity.oidc
refuses HS256 outright, because an HMAC-signed token is signed by anything holding the
client secret and the classic confusion attack presents the published RSA public key
as that secret. The two ends agree here so a misconfiguration fails at login rather
than becoming an accepted token.
ssoSessionMaxLifespan 36000 (10 hours) matches SESSION_ABSOLUTE_MAX in
brain.identity.sessions. If the realm allowed longer, a refresh loop would keep a
March sign-in alive in September on the Keycloak side while our own registry refused
it, and the mismatch would present as random logouts rather than as a policy.
revokeRefreshToken true with refreshTokenMaxReuse 0 makes a stolen refresh token
detectable: replaying one invalidates the chain. Without it a copied refresh token is
a ten-hour credential with no way to notice it was taken.
directAccessGrantsEnabled false everywhere. The password grant skips the browser flow,
which means it skips the second factor and every conditional step configured in it. A
flow whose checks can be bypassed by asking a different endpoint is not a flow.
implicitFlowEnabled false, standardFlowEnabled true, PKCE S256 required on the public
console client. The implicit flow puts the token in a URL fragment, which lands in
browser history and referrer headers.
GROUPS CARRY ROLES AND NEVER CAPABILITIES. The groups below map to the six platform
roles in brain.identity.roles through GroupRoleRule, and to nothing else. There is
deliberately no group, attribute or client role here that names a capability: putting
one in this file would move the answer to 'who can read the margin on this client'
into a directory that nobody in this company reviews.
A SECOND FACTOR IS WRITTEN INTO THE TOKEN, AND UNTIL 2026-09-17 IT WAS NOT.
brain.identity.bearer.assurance_from gives Assurance.STRONG, the only level that may
exercise an admin: or approve: capability, to a token whose amr claim names a second
factor. Keycloak 26.0 mints no amr by default: no built-in client scope carries an amr
mapper, and oidc-amr-mapper writes only the reference value configured on each step the
person completed (default.reference.value), and only while that step is younger than
default.reference.maxAge, which counts as 0 when absent. This realm had none of the
three, so no install could mint a strong token, and every admin screen refused everybody,
a person who had set up OTP included. Found on the owner's staging install.
So brain-identity carries the amr mapper, and the browser flow below is Keycloak's own
built-in browser flow reproduced step for step with a reference on two steps: pwd on the
password form and otp on the OTP form, each valid for the ten-hour session. It is
declared under the built-in alias 'browser' rather than copied under a new name. The
import builds every built-in flow this file does not declare, so a renamed copy would
leave a second, unreferenced browser flow one binding away from being used. And an
install imported before this change is repaired by adding the same two references to the
'browser' flow it already has, so a fresh install and a repaired one end up the same
shape. docs/install/authentication.md has those steps.

groups.name: brain
groups._comment: A container, mapped to nothing. Membership of /brain alone confers no role.

subGroups.name: department-admin
_comment: Never mapped itself. department_admin is in SCOPE_REQUIRED, so a rule for it
must carry a scope, and only the per-department children below can supply one.
A rule for the bare parent would be a company-wide admin created by a group.

subGroups.name: approver
subGroups._comment: Also scope-required. Same rule as department-admin: children only.

clientScopes.name: brain-identity
clientScopes.description: The claims brain.identity.oidc.ClaimMapping reads. Nothing else.

config._comment: Keycloak 25 moved sub out of the access token into its built-in basic scope. A full import replaces the client scope set with the one this file declares, so naming that built-in on the client would be discarded exactly as openid, profile and email were on 2026-09-06. Minting it from this realm's own scope is the only spelling that survives an import. Without it every token is refused as missing_claim and nobody signs in.

config.claim.name: groups
config._comment: full.path true because GroupRoleRule compares the whole path exactly; a bare leaf name would make /brain/approver/web and /clientx/approver/web the same string.

protocolMappers.name: amr
protocolMappers._comment: The authentication methods the sign-in used, which brain.identity.bearer.assurance_from reads to decide between AUTHENTICATED and STRONG. Here on brain-identity for the reason the audience mapper below is: brain-console carries this scope by default, so every token issued to the console gets it. Access token only, because the access token is what the console sends and what the API validates; the console never reads its ID token. access.token.claim is spelled out because OIDCAttributeMapperHelper.includeInAccessToken is "true".equals(value), so an absent key is off. The values come from the authenticatorConfig entries the browser flow names, and a step with no reference contributes nothing.

protocolMappers.name: brain-api-audience
protocolMappers._comment: Without an explicit audience mapper, a token minted for the console carries no aud for the API, and validate_token refuses it. That refusal is correct: a token is issued for a party, and accepting one issued for somebody else is the confused deputy. This sits on the brain-identity client scope rather than on brain-api's own protocolMappers, where it was first written. A dedicated mapper applies to tokens issued FOR that client, and brain-api has standardFlow, directAccess, serviceAccounts and implicit all disabled, so no token is ever issued for it and the mapper could never fire. The comment above described precisely the failure its own placement guaranteed: every console sign-in would have completed at Keycloak and then been refused by validate_token for WRONG_AUDIENCE. brain-console carries brain-identity as a default client scope, so here it applies to exactly the tokens that need it.

clients.name: Company Brain console
clients.description: The browser app. Public client, authorisation code with PKCE.
_comment: brain-identity alone, and the three that used to sit beside it are gone.
This file previously listed openid, profile and email here. The first real import,
on 2026-09-06 against Keycloak 26.0, logged three warnings: 'Referenced client scope
openid doesn't exist. Ignoring', and the same for profile and email. They were
ignored because a full realm import replaces the client scope set with the one this
file declares, and this file declares only brain-identity. openid was wrong in a
second way as well: it is a scope value a client asks for in the request, never a
client scope an administrator defines.
Removing them changes no behaviour, because Keycloak was already discarding them.
What it changes is that the import is now silent, and an import that prints warnings
is one where the next person cannot tell the harmless lines from the real ones.
Nothing is lost. brain.identity.oidc reads exactly two claims, groups and department,
and brain-identity maps both. profile and email would add name and email claims that
nothing in this system consumes. When something does want them, they are added
deliberately, as a declared scope with its mappers, rather than as a name that
resolves to nothing.
webOrigins is an explicit origin and never '*' or '+'. A wildcard here lets any
site read a token from this realm.
backchannel.logout.session.required true makes Keycloak send the sid, which is
what SessionRegistry.end_session needs; end_all_for covers the case where it does
not arrive or the session was never seen by this replica.
redirectUris name the deployment this realm is imported into, and the risk is real:
a stale redirect URI in a realm import is an open redirect, because Keycloak will
hand a code to any address listed here. So they are exact paths rather than a
wildcard, there are only two, and the second is localhost for development.
https://origin.not-configured.example is a placeholder and not an address. It
appears four times, here, in webOrigins, in backchannel.logout.url and in
post.logout.redirect.uris, and brain.ops.realm_import.importable_realm replaces
every one of them with this installation's own origin on the way into Keycloak.
That is why they cannot drift apart: they are one value written four times rather
than four values somebody has to remember to change together.
It named one deployment's host until 2026-09-09, and the consequence was not
cosmetic. Keycloak matches redirect_uri exactly against this list, so a second
client importing this realm got an allowlist naming somebody else's server: their
console's sign-in was refused at Keycloak with 'Invalid parameter: redirect_uri',
before the login form, and nothing near that page said why. The origin is
configuration and it is INSTALL_OIDC_REDIRECT_URIS, which brain.install declares
required with no default for exactly this reason.
The placeholder is a reserved documentation domain, so it can never resolve and can
never be registered, and importable_realm refuses to emit a realm that still
carries it. A plausible-looking default host here would be the same defect with a
different spelling: it would import, and sign-in would fail somewhere else.

clients.name: Company Brain API
clients.description: The audience every token this system accepts is minted for.
clients._comment: No dedicated mappers, deliberately. The brain-api-audience mapper lived here and could never fire: a dedicated mapper applies to tokens issued for its own client, and every flow on this one is disabled because it is a resource server that nobody signs in to. It now sits on the brain-identity client scope, which brain-console carries by default.

clients.name: Example service account
clients.description: A machine caller. Client credentials only; no browser flow at all.
_comment: No secret is stored in this file and none ever should be. kcadm prints one on
creation; it belongs in OpenBao.
use.refresh.tokens false: a client-credentials caller can ask for a new token
whenever it likes, so a refresh token is a second long-lived credential with no
purpose.
This client's tokens carry no sid, which is how brain.identity.sessions keeps the
interactive and service paths disjoint. The owner, ceiling and expiry live in our
own ServiceAccount record, not here: Keycloak knows the robot exists, and this
system decides what it may borrow.
Template for M1.1.4, disabled and pointed at .invalid. A client's SAML IdP is added
per deployment; brain.identity.oidc.SamlFederation is the reviewed shape of these
same fields, and it refuses the two settings that are always got wrong:
wantAssertionsSigned false and validateSignature false, either of which turns an
assertion into a form post claiming to be a person.
principalType ATTRIBUTE with a stable attribute, never a transient NameID: a
transient identifier changes every session, so nobody would be recognised twice and
principal_for would return UnmappedSubject to the same person every morning.
pwd is RFC 8176's value for a password, and brain.identity.bearer does not count it as
a second factor. It is written at all so that a password-only token says so: without
it that token and one from a realm whose amr mapper never ran both carry an empty amr,
and decoding a token, the one diagnostic an administrator has, could not tell a missing
second factor from a missing mapper.
otp is in brain.identity.bearer.SECOND_FACTOR_METHODS, which is what turns a sign-in
that passed this step into Assurance.STRONG.
maxAge is the reason this was not one line. AmrUtils.isAmrValid keeps a reference only
while authTime + maxAge >= now, and an absent maxAge is read as 0, so a reference with
no maxAge is gone from every token minted a second after the step: the first access
token already lacks it. 36000 seconds is ssoSessionMaxLifespan, so the second factor
presented at sign-in counts for every token that session mints, refreshes included, and
no longer, because the session cannot outlive it. That is the meaning
A_SECOND_FACTOR_IS_A_CLAIM_ABOUT_THIS_SESSION gives the claim. A shorter value would be a
step-up policy, which is a decision somebody should argue for rather than a default.
Keycloak 26.0.0's DefaultAuthenticationFlows.browserFlow, step for step, as a realm
imported without authenticationFlows was given it: the same aliases, requirements and
priorities, Kerberos disabled because this realm requires no Kerberos credential, and
the Organization step because the organization feature is on by default in 26.0 and the
built-in flow adds it to every realm but master. The only additions are the two
authenticatorConfig references on the password form and the OTP form.
Declaring it changes nothing else about the import. DefaultExportImportManager imports
the flows this file declares and then calls DefaultAuthenticationFlows.migrateFlows,
which builds every built-in flow still missing by alias: direct grant, registration,
reset credentials, clients, first broker login, saml ecp and docker auth all arrive as
before. No model migration runs on this import, because they run only for a file that
names a keycloakVersion, and this one names none.
Every authenticatorConfig and flowAlias named here has to be declared in this file. The
import looks each one up by alias before migrateFlows has built anything, and a name it
cannot find stops the import with nothing in the log near the login page.

authenticationFlows.description: Flow to determine if the organization identity-first login is to be used
Username, password, otp and other auth forms.
Flow to determine if the OTP is required for the authentication

requiredActions.name: Configure OTP
requiredActions._comment: defaultAction true so a new account is asked to set up a second factor at first login. Assurance.STRONG is what brain.gate.admission requires for approve and admin, so without this nobody can approve anything. Setting one up is not presenting one: this action runs after the flow, so the OTP form was not a completed step of the session it ran in, and that session's tokens carry pwd alone. The person signs out and signs in again, and that sign-in passes the OTP form and carries otp.
